questionEn: In Surah Ghafir 40:7-8, who makes the supplication 'Rabbana wasi'ta kulla shay'in rahmatan wa 'ilman' seeking forgiveness and Paradise for repentant believers and their families?
optionsEn: The angels who bear the Throne and those around it
The prophets gathered at Al-Masjid al-Aqsa
The believing jinn
The martyrs of Uhud
explanationEn: The angels carrying the Throne and surrounding it glorify Allah and supplicate for believers, asking Allah to admit them and their righteous parents, spouses, and offspring into Gardens of Eden.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Ahqaf 46:15, at what milestone age does the Qur'an depict a righteous person praying to thank Allah for His favors upon themselves and their parents and to make their offspring righteous?
optionsEn: Seventy years of age
Sixty-three years of age
Twenty-five years of age
Forty years of age (balagha arba'ina sanah)
explanationEn: When a person reaches full maturity and attains forty years, the Qur'an describes this profound prayer of gratitude, righteousness, and repentance.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hashr 59:10, what inner disease do later generations of believers pray Allah NOT place in their hearts toward those who preceded them in faith?
optionsEn: Rancor or malice (ghill) toward those who believed
Attachment to travel
Forgetfulness of prayer
Fear of poverty
explanationEn: After praising the Muhajirun and Ansar, Allah praises later believers who pray for those before them and ask: 'Do not put in our hearts any resentment/rancor toward those who have believed.'

questionEn: Which two verses in Surah Al-Mumtahanah (60:4-5) present an exemplary du'a of Prophet Ibrahim and his companions regarding reliance on Allah and turning back to Him?
optionsEn: Asking to divide the sea
Saying 'Our Lord, upon You we have relied, and to You we have returned, and to You is the destination'
Asking for wings to escape Babylon
Asking for rain during drought
explanationEn: Allah holds up Ibrahim and those with him as an excellent example (uswatun hasanah), quoting their prayer of total reliance on Allah and plea not to be made a trial for disbelievers.

questionEn: On the Day of Judgment, what do the believers pray regarding their spiritual light in Surah At-Tahrim 66:8?
optionsEn: 'Our Lord, lend our light to the hypocrites'
'Our Lord, dim the sun and stars'
'Our Lord, make our light brighter than the angels'
'Our Lord, perfect for us our light and forgive us'
explanationEn: As their light proceeds before them and on their right hands (while the hypocrites' light is extinguished), believers earnestly pray for Allah to perfect their light and forgive them.

questionEn: Who uttered the Qur'anic supplication 'Rabbi-bni li 'indaka baytan fil-jannah' ('My Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise')?
optionsEn: Maryam, mother of 'Isa
Asiyah, the believing wife of Pharaoh
The mother of Prophet Musa
Bilqis, Queen of Sheba
explanationEn: Allah presents Pharaoh's wife as a model for believers, quoting her prayer asking first for proximity to Allah ('indaka — near You) before the house in Paradise, and deliverance from Pharaoh.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Falaq (113:1-5), which specific hidden evils does the believer seek refuge from with the Lord of Daybreak?
optionsEn: Hunger, thirst, poverty, and debt
Floods, earthquakes, locusts, and drought
Forgetfulness, anger, laziness, and cowardice
Created evil, darkness when it settles, blowers on knots (sorcerers), and the envier when he envies
explanationEn: Surah Al-Falaq seeks refuge from external harms: the evil of creation, the encroaching darkness, those who practice magic by blowing on knots, and the envier's active envy.

questionEn: What specific internal threat does Surah An-Nas (114:1-6) teach the believer to seek refuge from with the Lord, Sovereign, and God of mankind?
optionsEn: The noise of markets
False witnesses in courts
Physical fatigue during pilgrimage
The retreating whisperer (al-waswasil-khannas) who whispers into human chests
explanationEn: Surah An-Nas seeks protection from the retreating whisperer—from among both jinn and humans—who whispers evil into the hearts/chests of people.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Fatihah (1:6-7), how does the Qur'an characterize the Straight Path (As-Sirat al-Mustaqim) that Muslims pray for in every rak'ah of prayer?
optionsEn: The path of wealth and long life
The path of monastic isolation
The path of those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor, not of those who earned wrath or went astray
The path leading solely to Mount Sinai
explanationEn: Surah Al-Fatihah defines the Straight Path as the way of the blessed (prophets, truthful, martyrs, and righteous), distinct from those who knew truth and rejected it or strayed in ignorance.

questionEn: In Surah Al-An'am 6:162, what comprehensive dedication of life and worship is the Prophet commanded to declare?
optionsEn: My prayer, my rites of sacrifice, my living, and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the worlds
My songs and poetry belong to my tribe
My trade and travels belong to Makkah
Only my fasting belongs to the sacred months
explanationEn: The declaration 'Inna salati wa nusuki wa mahyaya wa mamati lillahi Rabbil-'alamin' encapsulates complete devotion to Allah alone.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:285-286, what concise phrase of obedience did the Messenger and believers utter immediately before the closing prayers of forgiveness?
optionsEn: 'We hear and we obey (sami'na wa ata'na); Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return'
'We rely solely upon our tribal treaties'
'We ask first for signs in the heavens'
'We hear and we wait until morning'
explanationEn: After affirming belief in Allah, His angels, Books, and Messengers without distinction, the believers declare 'Sami'na wa ata'na, ghufranaka Rabbana wa ilaykal-masir.'

questionEn: In Surah Al-A'raf 7:155, when seventy chosen men of Bani Isra'il were seized by a tremor at the appointed meeting, how did Prophet Musa appeal to Allah?
optionsEn: He asked: 'Would You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done?' and sought forgiveness and mercy
He vowed never to return to Egypt
He asked for the sea to part a second time
He blamed the seventy elders for doubting him
explanationEn: Musa acknowledged that it was Allah's trial by which He guides or leaves astray whom He wills, calling Allah their Protector (Waliyy) and the Best of Forgivers.

questionEn: In Surah Ta-Ha 20:45-46, when Musa and Harun expressed fear that Pharaoh might hasten to harm them, what reassurance did Allah give them?
optionsEn: 'Fear not; indeed, I am with you both — I hear and I see'
That Pharaoh would die before they arrived
That an earthquake would destroy the palace first
That they should travel only at night in disguise
explanationEn: Allah comforted Musa and Harun with His divine companionship ('Innani ma'akuma asma'u wa ara') and instructed them to speak gently to Pharaoh.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:17, what happens in the parable of the hypocrites who are compared to one who kindled a fire (istawqada naran)?
optionsEn: The fire guided them safely to a lush oasis
The fire burned their crops and turned into silver
A cool breeze turned the flames into shade
Once the fire illuminated around him, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness unable to see
explanationEn: Hypocrites momentarily benefited from the outward light of Islam, but because of their inner disbelief Allah removed their light, leaving them deaf, dumb, and blind in darkness.

questionEn: In the second parable of the hypocrites in Surah Al-Baqarah 2:19-20 (the heavy rainstorm from the sky), why do they put their fingers into their ears?
optionsEn: To block out the noise of the marketplace
From the thunderclaps in fear of death
To sleep undisturbed during the storm
To avoid hearing the call to charity
explanationEn: Overwhelmed by darkness, thunder, and lightning—symbolizing the Qur'an's warnings—they thrust their fingers in their ears fearing death, while lightning almost snatches away their sight.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:26, what small creature does Allah mention to affirm that He does not shy away from presenting any parable, whether of it or what is beyond it?
optionsEn: A gnat/mosquito (ba'udah)
An ant
A locust
A moth
explanationEn: When critics mocked parables mentioning flies or spiders, Allah declared He is not ashamed to cite even a mosquito—which guides believers further while misguiding only the defiantly disobedient.

questionEn: Why does Surah Al-Baqarah 2:74 say the hardened hearts of Bani Isra'il became 'like stones, or even harder'?
optionsEn: Because stones reflect sunlight at dawn
Because stones can be carved into pillars
Because stones melt quickly in summer heat
Because some stones gush forth rivers, split for water, or fall down out of fear of Allah
explanationEn: Unlike hardened hearts untouched by reminders, even solid rocks respond to Allah's command by yielding springs, splitting open, or tumbling in awe of Him.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:171, calling disbelievers who refuse to reflect is compared to a shepherd calling out to what?
optionsEn: Animals that hear nothing except indistinct shouts and cries
Mountains that echo every word clearly
Birds migrating high above the clouds
Waves crashing against a harbor wall
explanationEn: Just as livestock hear only the sound of a voice without grasping the meaning of words, those clinging blindly to falsehood hear the sound of revelation without understanding.

questionEn: In the famous parable of charity in Surah Al-Baqarah 2:261, what is the total yield described for a single grain planted in Allah's cause?
optionsEn: Ten grains from two stalks
Twelve baskets of barley
Seven ears, each containing a hundred grains (700-fold, and more for whom He wills)
Fortyfold in one season
explanationEn: Spending wealth in Allah's path is likened to one seed that grows seven spikes, each bearing a hundred grains—700-fold multiplication, and Allah multiplies even further.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:264, charity ruined by reminders of generosity (mann) and hurtful words (adha) is compared to what happens when heavy rain strikes what object?
optionsEn: A clay jar buried in sand
A smooth rock (safwan) covered with a thin layer of dust, leaving it completely bare
A wooden bridge over a river
A fertile orchard on a hilltop
explanationEn: Just as a downpour washes away dust from a bare rock leaving nothing behind, ostentation and mistreatment wipe out the spiritual reward of charity.

questionEn: By contrast, in Surah Al-Baqarah 2:265, sincere charity seeking Allah's pleasure is compared to a garden on elevated ground (bi-rabwah) that produces what when struck by heavy rain?
optionsEn: Salt crystals along its borders
Only bitter wild herbs
Double its normal fruit—and even if heavy rain misses it, a gentle drizzle suffices
A single dry harvest
explanationEn: Because of its fertile elevated soil, sincere charity yields abundant reward under any circumstance—double under a downpour, and still fruitful even with a light drizzle.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:266, what catastrophe destroys the lush garden of an elderly man with weak children in the parable warning against losing all deeds on Judgment Day?
optionsEn: A flood of salt water from the sea
A swarm of desert locusts
A whirlwind containing fire (i'sarun fihi nar) that burns it completely
A sudden frost in late autumn
explanationEn: Ibn 'Abbas explained this parable refers to someone who performs good deeds then commits major sins at the end of life, losing everything at the exact moment of greatest need.

questionEn: In Surah Al-'Imran 3:117, what is the spending of disbelievers in this worldly life compared to?
optionsEn: Rain filling a cracked cistern
A ship sailing without a rudder
Gold buried in a collapsing cave
A freezing, biting wind (rihin fiha sirr) that strikes and ruins the harvest of a wrongdoing people
explanationEn: Instead of yielding lasting fruit in the Hereafter, what they spend out of opposition to truth destroys their spiritual harvest like an icy blast ruining crops.

questionEn: In Surah Al-An'am 6:122, how does the Qur'an contrast the guided believer with the one entrenched in misguidance?
optionsEn: A tall cedar tree versus a desert thorn
A skilled merchant versus an indebted farmer
One who was dead, brought to life, and given a light to walk among people versus one trapped in darkness
A fast runner versus a sleeping traveler
explanationEn: Guidance is depicted as resurrection from spiritual death and walking with illuminating clarity among society, whereas disbelief leaves one trapped in darkness.

questionEn: In Surah Al-A'raf 7:176, one who was given Allah's signs yet detached himself from them to follow his desires and Satan is compared to which animal?
optionsEn: A dog that pants whether you drive it away or leave it alone
A stubborn mule
A crow pecking at dry earth
A startled gazelle
explanationEn: Whether exhorted or left unaddressed, the one who abandons divine knowledge for base desires remains perpetually restless and panting after worldly lusts.

questionEn: In Surah Yunus 10:24, after rain makes the earth's vegetation lush and people think they have full mastery over it, what happens in the parable of worldly life?
optionsEn: Rivers carry its seeds across the ocean
The landowners divide it equally with angels
Allah's command comes by night or day, turning it into mown stubble as if it had not flourished yesterday
It remains evergreen for a hundred years
explanationEn: This vivid parable illustrates how swiftly worldly splendor and illusion of total human control vanish when Allah's decree arrives.

questionEn: Which two sensory pairs are contrasted in Surah Hud 11:24 to represent the disbelieving party and the believing party?
optionsEn: The silent and swift versus the loud and slow
The cold and weary versus the warm
The blind and deaf versus the seeing and hearing
The hungry and thirsty versus the full
explanationEn: Allah asks: 'Are the two parties equal in comparison?'—likening those who reject revelation to the blind and deaf, and believers to those who clearly see and hear.

questionEn: In Surah Ar-Ra'd 13:14, calling upon false deities who cannot respond is compared to a person doing what?
optionsEn: Whispering into a closed copper vessel
Stretching out his palms toward water so it reaches his mouth, yet it never reaches it
Waiting for snow in midsummer
Digging in solid granite with a reed
explanationEn: Water cannot rise into an outstretched hand merely by wishing or beckoning; likewise, false gods are utterly powerless to answer those who supplicate to them.

questionEn: In the parable of truth and falsehood in Surah Ar-Ra'd 13:17 (rain filling valleys and metal smelted in fire), what happens to the foam (zabad) versus what benefits people?
optionsEn: The foam turns into pearls while the water evaporates
The foam settles at the bottom of the valley
Both the foam and the water remain permanently
The foam vanishes as discarded scum, while what benefits mankind remains on the earth
explanationEn: Falsehood may appear loud and puffed up like surface foam on floodwaters or slag on molten ore, yet it quickly dissipates while enduring truth stays.

questionEn: In Surah Ibrahim 14:18, what are the deeds of those who disbelieve in their Lord compared to on a stormy day?
optionsEn: Footprints carved into marble
Dry leaves floating on a calm pond
Ashes upon which the wind blows fiercely (ka-ramadin-ishtaddat bihir-rih)
Clouds gathering before dawn
explanationEn: On the Day of Judgment, deeds devoid of faith scatter completely like fine ashes caught in a violent gale, leaving them with zero control over what they earned.

questionEn: How does Surah Ibrahim 14:26 describe the 'evil word' (kalimah khabithah) in contrast to the good tree?
optionsEn: Like a thorny vine climbing a cedar
Like an evil tree uprooted from above the earth, having no stability
Like a hollow reed beside a pond
Like a withered branch left in winter
explanationEn: Falsehood lacks deep roots and genuine foundation; like a torn-up tree lying on the surface, it has no permanence or stability.

questionEn: In Surah An-Nahl 16:75, Allah presents a parable comparing an owned slave who has power over nothing with whom?
optionsEn: A child playing by the seashore
One whom Allah provided with goodly provision who spends from it secretly and openly
A weary traveler lost in a canyon
A blacksmith working near a furnace
explanationEn: Asking 'Are they equal?', this parable refutes equating powerless idols with the Sovereign Creator who freely bestows and disposes of all provision.

questionEn: In Surah An-Nahl 16:76, what contrasts with a person who is dumb, powerless over anything, and a complete burden upon his master?
optionsEn: One who speaks ten languages
One who builds high towers of stone
One who owns ships on every sea
One who commands justice and is upon a straight path
explanationEn: This second parable in An-Nahl highlights the absurdity of worshipping mute, helpless idols instead of Allah, who commands absolute justice and truth.

questionEn: In Surah An-Nahl 16:92, breaking solemn oaths and covenants after confirming them is compared to what foolish act?
optionsEn: Planting seeds on polished marble
Pouring water into a woven basket
A woman unraveling her spun yarn into untwisted strands after having spun it strong
Lighting a lantern in bright midday
explanationEn: Just as it is senseless to spend hours spinning strong thread only to untwist it back into loose fibers, breaking solemn covenants ruins one's moral integrity and trust.

questionEn: In Surah An-Nahl 16:112, what did Allah make a safe, tranquil, and abundantly provisioned town taste after it was ungrateful for His blessings?
optionsEn: The garment of hunger and fear (libasal-ju'i wal-khawf)
A flood of snow and ice
Eternal darkness at noon
Silence across its harbors
explanationEn: Because of their ingratitude and rejection, security and abundance were completely inverted so that hunger and fear enveloped them like a tight garment.

questionEn: In the parable of the two men in Surah Al-Kahf 18:32-42, what surrounded the two lush gardens of grapevines belonging to the arrogant owner?
optionsEn: Dry salt flats on all sides
Date palms, with grain crops in between and a river flowing through them
Olive groves and cypress trees
Iron walls and watchtowers
explanationEn: Despite being blessed with abundant vines, date palms, grain, and flowing water, he boasted his garden would never perish and doubted the Hour—until ruin struck overnight.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Kahf 18:45, what happens to the earth's lush vegetation after it mingles with rain sent from the sky?
optionsEn: It sinks beneath the earth intact
It freezes into crystal
It turns into dry broken fragments (hashiman) scattered by the winds
It turns into towering forests that outlive kingdoms
explanationEn: Following the fleeting beauty of worldly life, plants dry up into brittle chaff blown away by the wind, reminding believers that enduring righteous deeds are far better.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hajj 22:31, what is the spiritual state of one who associates partners with Allah (shirk) compared to?
optionsEn: Walking barefoot over warm sand
Falling from the sky and being snatched by birds or blown by wind into a remote place
Climbing a ladder in daylight
Rowing a small boat near the shore
explanationEn: Abandoning pure Tawhid plunges a soul from lofty spiritual certainty into utter helplessness, torn apart by competing passions and swept far from safety.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hajj 22:73, what humble creature does the Qur'an declare false deities could never create—even if all of them banded together—nor recover anything from if it snatched it away?
optionsEn: A fly (dhubab)
A honeybee
A cricket
A beetle
explanationEn: Calling them weak in both seeking and being sought, Allah exposes the absolute powerlessness of idols that cannot even create a tiny fly or reclaim food from it.

questionEn: In the famous Parable of Light (Ayat an-Nur, 24:35), what is the lamp (misbah) inside the glass (zujajah) compared to, and what tree fuels it?
optionsEn: Like lightning at dusk, fueled by palm oil
Like the crescent moon, fueled by a cedar tree
Like a brilliant pearly star (kawkabun durriyy), lit from a blessed olive tree neither eastern nor western
Like a blazing torch, fueled by pine resin
explanationEn: The olive tree receives balanced sunlight throughout the day—neither solely eastern nor western—producing oil so pure it almost glows before fire even touches it: 'Light upon light.'

questionEn: In Surah An-Nur 24:39, what are the seemingly impressive deeds of disbelievers compared to for a desperate, thirsty traveler?
optionsEn: A locked well with a broken rope
Salt water bubbling in a spring
A mirage in a lowland (sarabin bi-qi'ah) that looks like water until he arrives and finds nothing
Rain falling only behind distant hills
explanationEn: Just as a mirage deceives a parched traveler from afar and vanishes upon arrival, deeds done without faith yield nothing on Judgment Day except Allah settling their full account.

questionEn: In the second parable of Surah An-Nur 24:40, what compounds the darkness experienced by a disbeliever in 'a deep fathomless sea' (bahrin lujjiyy)?
optionsEn: Smoke from distant ships
Dense fog over coastal cliffs
Eclipses occurring every hour
Wave topped by another wave, and dark clouds above them—darkness upon darkness
explanationEn: Layered under deep ocean water, double waves, and thick storm clouds, one cannot even see his own outstretched hand—illustrating that whoever Allah gives no light has no light.

questionEn: In Surah Al-'Ankabut 29:41, what does Allah compare those who take protectors and allies other than Him to?
optionsEn: A silkworm spinning in autumn
A swallow nesting on sea cliffs
A spider building a house—for the frailest of all houses is the spider's house
A fox digging under shifting dunes
explanationEn: A spider's web offers no protection from heat, cold, wind, or predators; likewise, relying on false deities instead of Allah provides zero real security.

questionEn: In Surah Ar-Rum 30:28, how does Allah draw a parable 'from your own selves' to expose the absurdity of polytheism?
optionsEn: Asking whether you would make your own subordinates equal partners in your wealth, fearing them as you fear equals
Asking whether two captains can steer one ship in a storm
Asking whether two eyes can look in opposite directions
Asking whether a father gives his crown to a stranger
explanationEn: If humans themselves refuse to make their servants co-owners with equal authority over their own property, how much more absurd is it to assign Allah's own creation as partners in His sovereignty!

questionEn: In the Parable of the Companions of the Town (Ashab al-Qaryah) in Surah Ya-Sin 36:13-20, how many messengers were sent initially and who came running from the farthest end of the city?
optionsEn: Four angels disguised as merchants
Two messengers initially, reinforced by a third; then a believing man came running urging them to follow the messengers
Seven messengers arriving by ship
One messenger alone, supported by the city king
explanationEn: When the townspeople rejected the two messengers and then the third reinforcement, a sincere believing man hurried from the edge of the city testifying to the truth and was martyred into Paradise.

questionEn: In Surah Az-Zumar 39:29, what contrast does Allah draw to illustrate the peace of pure monotheism versus the chaos of polytheism?
optionsEn: A man belonging to quarreling, rival partners versus a man belonging wholly to one master
A straight highway versus a winding mountain trail
A quiet orchard versus a noisy bazaar
A single lantern versus a hundred dying candles
explanationEn: A servant pulled in conflicting directions by quarrelsome masters lives in constant confusion and distress, whereas serving One Lord brings clarity, harmony, and peace.

questionEn: In Surah Muhammad 47:12, how are disbelievers who indulge in worldly pleasure without regard for the Hereafter described?
optionsEn: They hoard coins like river magpies
They build nests like desert eagles
They enjoy themselves and eat just as grazing livestock eat (kama ta'kulul-an'am)
They sleep like hibernating bears
explanationEn: Whereas Allah admits believers into Gardens with flowing rivers, those who reject faith live purely for bodily consumption like cattle, unaware of the Fire awaiting them.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Fath 48:29, how is the community of the Prophet's followers described in the parable cited from the Injil (Gospel)?
optionsEn: Like gentle rain falling on terraced hills
Like stars emerging slowly after twilight
Like a crop that puts forth its shoot, strengthens it, grows thick, and stands straight on its stem
Like a flock of doves returning to Makkah
explanationEn: Starting small and vulnerable, the believing community steadily grew strong, cohesive, and firmly rooted—delighting the sowers and enraging the disbelievers.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hujurat 49:12, what shocking image does the Qur'an use to warn believers against backbiting (ghibah) one another?
optionsEn: Drinking polluted water from a ditch
Throwing stones at one's own reflection
Eating the flesh of one's dead brother
Burning one's own harvest at night
explanationEn: Allah asks: 'Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his brother when dead? You would detest it,' underscoring how vile it is to tarnish an absent brother's honor.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hadid 57:20, after listing five stages of worldly distraction (play, amusement, adornment, boasting, and rivalry in wealth/children), what seasonal parable does Allah give?
optionsEn: Rain whose resulting crops please the tillers, then dry, turn yellow, and crumble into debris (hutam)
A candle flickering in an open courtyard
Waves eroding a limestone cliff
Snow melting on a mountain ridge
explanationEn: Every fleeting worldly delight blooms briefly before turning yellow and crumbling away, contrasting with Allah's forgiveness and enduring pleasure.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hashr 59:16, what does Satan say to the human being in the parable illustrating how he abandons those he misled?
optionsEn: 'I never spoke a word to you'
'Let us divide the punishment equally'
'Indeed, I am disassociated from you; indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds'
'Wait for me at the gates of Paradise'
explanationEn: Just as Satan tells man 'Disbelieve' and then disowns him once he disbelieves, the hypocrites were deceived by allies who abandoned them to their doom.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hashr 59:21, what would have happened if Allah had sent down the Qur'an upon a mountain?
optionsEn: The mountain would have risen above the clouds
The mountain would have sprouted olive groves overnight
The mountain would have turned into solid gold
You would have seen it humbled and split asunder (khashi'an mutasaddi'an) out of fear of Allah
explanationEn: Allah says He presents these parables to humanity so they may reflect—contrasting the awe-struck response of a solid mountain with the heedlessness of hard human hearts.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Munafiqun 63:4, what does Allah compare the hypocrites to—impressing onlookers with their physical appearance and speech, yet devoid of living faith?
optionsEn: Brass statues standing in a courtyard
Pieces of propped-up timber (khushubun musannadah)
Dry reeds bending in the breeze
Painted clay jars filled with sand
explanationEn: Like cut planks propped against a wall—lifeless, unproductive, and hollow inside—they look impressive outwardly while thinking every shout is directed against them.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Mulk 67:22, how does the Qur'an contrast the misguided person with the one guided upon truth?
optionsEn: One carrying iron versus one carrying silk
One rowing upstream versus one floating downstream
One walking groveling upon his face versus one walking upright on a straight path
One walking in winter versus one resting in spring
explanationEn: Someone stumbling face-down cannot see where he is going and constantly falls, whereas the believer walks upright with clear vision along a straight, level road.

questionEn: In the Parable of the Owners of the Garden (Ashab al-Jannah) in Surah Al-Qalam 68:17-33, why was their bountiful orchard destroyed overnight?
optionsEn: They traded their crops for forbidden idols
They swore to harvest at dawn without saying 'If Allah wills' and plotted to exclude the poor from their share
They harvested their dates three weeks too early
They refused to irrigate their neighbors' fields
explanationEn: Refusing the rights of the needy and neglecting reliance on Allah, they awoke to find their garden black like a harvested night (kas-sarim), leading the wiser brother to urge repentance.

questionEn: In Surah Al-A'raf 7:179, why are people who have hearts that do not understand, eyes that do not see, and ears that do not hear said to be 'like cattle, rather even more astray'?
optionsEn: Because cattle follow their natural purpose and obey their Creator, whereas heedless humans waste intellect and free will
Because cattle live longer than humans
Because cattle gather near sacred waters
Because cattle migrate across continents every year
explanationEn: Animals fulfill the instinct and role Allah created them for, whereas humans gifted with reason and revelation who remain heedless sink lower by neglecting their higher purpose.

questionEn: In Surah Yunus 10:22, what happens to human sincerity in the parable of travelers aboard a ship struck by a gale and waves 'like canopies'?
optionsEn: They call upon every tribal idol in turn
They supplicate to Allah alone in complete sincerity, only to rebel unjustly once safely delivered to land
They argue over who owns the cargo
They throw all their food overboard immediately
explanationEn: Crisis strips away illusions and awakens innate Tawhid, yet once Allah rescues them to dry ground, many revert to ingratitude and transgression.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:275, how will those who consume Riba (usury/interest) rise on the Day of Resurrection?
optionsEn: Like one whom Satan has confounded and driven mad by his touch
Wearing garments woven from copper
Unable to open their eyes in the light
Carrying iron scales on their shoulders
explanationEn: Because they falsely equated usury with lawful trade, they will rise staggering in disarray as though struck into madness by Satan's touch.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Furqan 25:23, when Allah turns to the deeds of those who rejected revelation and mocked the messengers, what does He render those deeds into?
optionsEn: Scattered dust motes (haba'an manthura) floating in a beam of light
Empty parchment blown across the valley
Heavy stones sunk in the Red Sea
Charred charcoal beneath cold ash
explanationEn: Any outward charitable or impressive deeds lacking faith and sincerity carry no weight on the Day of Judgment, dispersing like weightless dust particles.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Anbiya 21:18, how does Allah describe the confrontation between truth and falsehood?
optionsEn: Falsehood slowly ages into truth
Truth waits patiently in a distant castle
Allah hurls truth against falsehood so it crushes its head, and falsehood vanishes
Truth and falsehood share the world in equal halves
explanationEn: Allah declares: 'Rather, We dash the truth upon falsehood, and it destroys it (fa-yadmaghuhu), and thereupon it departs.'

questionEn: In Surah Al-'Imran 3:103, what two metaphors express unity under Islam and the state from which Allah rescued the believers?
optionsEn: Sailing one ship and escaping a whirlpool
Holding fast to the Rope of Allah together and being saved from the brink of a pit of Fire
Holding a lantern and leaving a desert road
Building one stone wall and crossing a frozen river
explanationEn: United by faith in the Qur'an ('the Rope of Allah'), former enemies were reconciled as brothers and pulled back from the very edge of Hellfire.

questionEn: In Surah At-Tawbah 9:109, how does the Qur'an contrast a mosque built upon Taqwa with one built out of hypocrisy and division?
optionsEn: One filled at dawn versus one empty at noon
One built of cedar wood versus one built of reeds
One facing Makkah versus one facing Yemen
A foundation laid on Taqwa and Allah's pleasure versus a foundation on the edge of a crumbling cliff ready to collapse into Hellfire
explanationEn: A structure founded on righteousness stands firm, whereas Masjid Dirar—built to sow division—was like a building perched on an eroding cliff brink collapsing into Fire.

questionEn: In Surah Az-Zumar 39:42, what daily human experience is linked directly to death as a sign for people who reflect?
optionsEn: Hunger returning after every meal
Aging of hair from black to white
Forgetting dreams at sunrise
Sleep—when Allah takes souls temporarily, keeping those decreed for death and returning the rest for an appointed term
explanationEn: Sleep is depicted as a 'minor death' in which Allah holds full control over human souls, releasing them back to wakefulness until their final appointed term arrives.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Ahqaf 46:35 and Surah An-Nazi'at 79:46, how brief will the entire span of worldly life seem to disbelievers on the Day they witness the Hereafter?
optionsEn: Like a century of winter nights
Like a single hour of a day, or just an evening or its morning
Like seven full harvests
Like forty years in the wilderness
explanationEn: Measured against eternity and the awe of Judgment Day, decades of worldly existence shrink in memory to a fleeting hour or a single evening and its morning.

questionEn: In Surah Al-An'am 6:71, one who calls upon idols after Allah has guided them is compared to whom?
optionsEn: A watchman lighting a beacon on a hill
A merchant trading gold for silver
One whom devils lured bewildered in the earth while companions call him to guidance: 'Come to us!'
A swimmer diving into clear water
explanationEn: Torn between demonic misguidance pulling him off course and faithful companions calling him back to the straight road, only Allah's guidance provides true direction.

questionEn: In Surah Al-'Imran 3:7, how does the Qur'an distinguish 'Muhkamat' verses from 'Mutashabihat' verses?
optionsEn: Muhkamat are abrogated verses, while Mutashabihat are all legal verses
Muhkamat are clear, decisive verses forming the foundation of the Book, while Mutashabihat are open to multiple interpretations
Muhkamat are prose verses, while Mutashabihat are poetry
Muhkamat are revealed in Madinah, while Mutashabihat are revealed in Makkah
explanationEn: Surah Al-'Imran 3:7 explains that Muhkam verses are the core foundation (Umm al-Kitab) with clear meaning, whereas those with deviation in their hearts chase the Mutashabihat seeking discord.

questionEn: What is the famous exegetical maxim agreed upon by classical scholars regarding 'Asbab al-Nuzul' (occasions of revelation)?
optionsEn: A verse only applies to the single person it was revealed about
Every verse without a known occasion is invalid for legal rulings
Occasions of revelation override the Arabic wording of the text
Consideration is given to the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause (Al-'ibrah bi-'umum al-lafz la bi-khusus as-sabab)
explanationEn: While knowing the Sabab al-Nuzul clarifies context and wisdom, the general legal and moral ruling of a Qur'anic verse extends universally to everyone covered by its wording.

questionEn: In the methodology of 'Tafsir bil-Ma'thur' (narration-based exegesis), what is universally recognized as the highest and first source for explaining a Qur'anic verse?
optionsEn: Explaining the Qur'an by the Qur'an itself
Personal mystical intuition
Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry alone
Consulting ancient Greek philosophical texts
explanationEn: The hierarchy of Tafsir bil-Ma'thur begins with Tafsir al-Qur'an bil-Qur'an (what is brief in one place is detailed in another), followed by the Sunnah, then the Sahabah and Tabi'un.
reference: Ibn Kathir, Muqaddimah Tafsir al-Qur'an al-'Azim

questionEn: Which monumental classical work by Imam Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari is considered the foundational encyclopedia of early Tafsir bil-Ma'thur?
optionsEn: Ruh al-Ma'ani
Al-Kashshaf
Mafatih al-Ghayb
Jami' al-Bayan 'an Ta'wil Ay al-Qur'an
explanationEn: Imam al-Tabari (d. 310 AH) compiled isnad-backed narrations from the Prophet, Companions, and Successors alongside linguistic analysis in his celebrated Jami' al-Bayan.
reference: Al-Tabari, Jami' al-Bayan 'an Ta'wil Ay al-Qur'an

questionEn: What distinguishes praiseworthy 'Tafsir bir-Ra'y' (reason-based exegesis, mahmud) from blameworthy 'Tafsir bir-Ra'y' (madhmum)?
optionsEn: Praiseworthy Tafsir adheres strictly to Arabic linguistics, Qur'an, Sunnah, and scholarly principles rather than speaking out of whim or ignorance
Praiseworthy Tafsir relies solely on dreams
Blameworthy Tafsir quotes authentic Hadith
Blameworthy Tafsir uses Arabic grammar
explanationEn: Sound scholarly ijtihad grounded in the Arabic language and Sharia principles is welcomed, whereas interpreting the Qur'an by mere conjecture or sectarian desire is strictly forbidden.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:106, what principle does Allah affirm when He abrogates (naskh) a verse or causes it to be forgotten?
optionsEn: He brings something better than it or similar to it
He delegates revision of the law to angels
He removes an entire Surah from the Preserved Tablet
He leaves humanity without any replacement guidance
explanationEn: Naskh (legal abrogation during the Prophetic lifetime) reflects divine wisdom and gradual legislation, always substituting a ruling equal or more beneficial for the community.

questionEn: According to the majority of 'Ulum al-Qur'an scholars, what is the defining criterion separating a 'Makki' revelation from a 'Madani' revelation?
optionsEn: The dialect of the scribe who wrote it down
Whether the word 'Makkah' appears inside the Surah
Length of the Surah only
Time of revelation: before the Hijrah to Madinah is Makki, and after the Hijrah is Madani (regardless of location)
explanationEn: Thus, verses revealed at Mina or Arafat during the Farewell Pilgrimage—though geographically near Makkah—are classified as Madani because they came after the Hijrah.

questionEn: In Surah Az-Zukhruf 43:4 and Surah Ar-Ra'd 13:39, what title—meaning 'Mother of the Book'—refers to the celestial original record with Allah?
optionsEn: Al-Mithaq
Al-Mawqut
Umm al-Kitab
Al-Mu'allaqat
explanationEn: 'Umm al-Kitab' in these verses refers to the Preserved Tablet with Allah from which all revelation originates (the term is also applied in 3:7 to Muhkam verses and to Surah Al-Fatihah).

questionEn: How many Surahs in the Noble Qur'an open with 'Al-Huruf al-Muqatta'at' (disjointed letters such as Alif-Lam-Mim or Ya-Sin)?
optionsEn: 7 Surahs
14 Surahs
40 Surahs
29 Surahs
explanationEn: Exactly 29 Surahs begin with these 14 distinct Arabic letters, demonstrating the Qur'an's linguistic miracle composed from the very alphabet Arabs already knew yet could not rival.

questionEn: Which two Surahs begin with the longest five-letter combinations of Huruf al-Muqatta'at?
optionsEn: Al-A'raf and Yunus
Maryam (Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad) and Ash-Shura (Ha-Mim, 'Ayn-Sin-Qaf)
Al-Baqarah and Al-'Imran
Yusuf and Ibrahim
explanationEn: Surah Maryam (19:1) opens with five letters in one verse, while Surah Ash-Shura (42:1-2) opens with two verses totaling five letters; the shortest are single-letter openings in Sad, Qaf, and Nun.

questionEn: What progressive challenge (Tahaddi) did the Qur'an issue to skeptics who claimed it was humanly authored?
optionsEn: Recite it backwards from Surah An-Nas
Produce something like the whole Qur'an, then ten fabricated surahs, and finally even a single surah like it
Memorize all 114 surahs in one night
Translate it into Latin within one year
explanationEn: Allah challenged humans and jinn combined to produce a book like it (17:88), then ten surahs (11:13), then a single surah (10:38 & 2:23)—proving its unmatched divine inimitability (I'jaz).
reference: Surah Al-Isra 17:88; Surah Hud 11:13; Surah Al-Baqarah 2:23

questionEn: In Surah Al-Furqan 25:32, what wisdom did Allah give in reply to disbelievers who asked why the Qur'an was not sent down all at once?
optionsEn: Because angels could only carry one verse per month
Because paper was scarce in Makkah
So that Allah might strengthen the Prophet's heart thereby and reveal it in measured stages (tartila)
To hide the text from neighboring tribes
explanationEn: Gradual revelation (tanjim) over ~23 years continuously comforted the Prophet's heart, addressed real events as they unfolded, and facilitated memorization and gradual practice.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hijr 15:9, what unconditional promise did Allah make regarding the Qur'anic text itself?
optionsEn: That parchment manuscripts would never fade
That Allah Himself sent down the Reminder and will surely be its Guardian
That every scribe would live to a hundred years
That no foreign language would ever translate it
explanationEn: 'Inna Nahnu nazzalna-dh-dhikra wa inna lahu lahafizun' guarantees the Qur'an's textual preservation across generations through mass memorization and meticulous written transmission.

questionEn: Why did Surah An-Nahl 16:103 refute the Makkan claim that a certain human foreigner was teaching the Prophet (peace be upon him) the Qur'an?
optionsEn: Because the tongue of the one they alluded to was foreign (a'jamiyy), whereas this Qur'an is in clear Arabic (lisanin 'arabiyyin mubin)
Because the Prophet never left his home
Because the foreigner lived in Abyssinia
Because the foreigner was blind
explanationEn: It was impossible for someone speaking broken or non-Arabic to produce the pinnacle of Arabic eloquence that stunned even the greatest Arab poets.

questionEn: Under Caliph Abu Bakr (RA), who led the team that compiled the written Qur'an into a single bound volume (suhuf) after many memorizers were martyred at the Battle of Yamamah?
optionsEn: Salman al-Farisi
Bilal ibn Rabah
Zayd ibn Thabit
Khalid ibn al-Walid
explanationEn: Upon 'Umar's suggestion, Abu Bakr entrusted Zayd ibn Thabit—the Prophet's chief revelation scribe—to verify every verse through both written records and living memory.

questionEn: Why did Caliph 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (RA) later commission standardized copies of the Mushaf (Al-Mushaf al-Imam) to be sent to major Muslim provinces?
optionsEn: Because the original pages in Madinah were lost in a flood
Because Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman warned that Muslims in distant regions were disputing over differences in recitation
To replace Arabic script with Syriac script
To shorten the longer Madani surahs
explanationEn: After Hudhayfah observed soldiers from Iraq and Syria arguing over recitations during campaigns, 'Uthman united the Ummah upon the authentic Qurayshi standard copies compiled by Zayd ibn Thabit and others.

questionEn: According to Surah Yusuf 12:111 and Surah Hud 11:120, what are the primary purposes of Qur'anic narratives (Al-Qasas al-Qur'ani)?
optionsEn: To provide a lesson for people of understanding ('ibrah) and make firm the Prophet's heart
To record royal tax archives
To entertain travelers at night
To teach ancient architectural measurements
explanationEn: Qur'anic stories are never mere entertainment; they serve as spiritual lessons confirming earlier revelations, strengthening hearts, and guiding believers.

questionEn: Which two honorable titles does the Qur'an give to Angel Jibril in Surah An-Nahl 16:102 and Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:193?
optionsEn: Ruh al-Qudus (The Pure/Holy Spirit) and Ar-Ruh al-Amin (The Trustworthy Spirit)
Malik and Zabaniyah
Malak al-Mawt and Al-Muntaqim
Raqib and 'Atid
explanationEn: Allah describes Jibril as 'Ruh al-Qudus' who brings down truth to strengthen believers, and 'Ar-Ruh al-Amin' who brought the clear Arabic Qur'an down upon the Prophet's heart.

questionEn: Which two angels are explicitly named together in Surah Al-Baqarah 2:98 with the warning that whoever is an enemy to them has Allah as an enemy?
optionsEn: Israfil and Malik
Harut and Marut
Munkar and Nakir
Jibril and Mika'il
explanationEn: When some people claimed Jibril was their enemy while Mika'il was their friend, Allah declared that hostility toward Allah, His angels, Messengers, Jibril, or Mika'il makes one an enemy of Allah.

questionEn: In Surah Az-Zukhruf 43:77, who is the chief angel guarding Hellfire to whom the inhabitants cry out asking Allah to put an end to them?
optionsEn: Ridwan
Mika'il
Jibril
Malik
explanationEn: They call out, 'O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us!' and after a long duration he responds, 'Indeed, you will remain.'

questionEn: In Surah Al-Infitar 82:10-12, how does the Qur'an describe the guardian angels appointed over every human being?
optionsEn: Noble Recorders (Kiraman Katibin) who know whatever you do
Angels who descend only on Fridays
Messengers who appear exclusively in dreams
Silent Watchers who record only spoken oaths
explanationEn: Allah reminds humanity that appointed over them are noble, honorable scribes carefully documenting every action.

questionEn: What precision in angelic recording is highlighted in Surah Qaf 50:17-18?
optionsEn: Only major crimes are noted once a year
Only the leaders of nations have recording angels
Thoughts of charity are erased unless spoken aloud
Not a single word does a person utter except that with him is an observer prepared to record ('raqibun 'atid')
explanationEn: Two angels seated on the right and left carefully note every utterance, prompting righteous awareness of every word spoken.

questionEn: In Surah As-Sajdah 32:11, who is stated to be entrusted with taking human souls at the time of death?
optionsEn: The Angel of Death (Malak al-Mawt) who has been put in charge of you
Each person's own shadow
A wind from the east
The angel of mountains
explanationEn: Allah says: 'The Angel of Death who has been entrusted with you will take your souls, then to your Lord you will be returned.'

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:102, what warning did the two angels Harut and Marut give in Babylon before anyone learned sorcery from them?
optionsEn: 'Only kings may study these words'
'We are only a trial (fitnah), so do not disbelieve'
'Pay gold before speaking to us'
'Use this knowledge to build temples'
explanationEn: Sent as a moral test in Babylon, Harut and Marut explicitly warned people against disbelief, yet people chose to learn what harmed them—such as causing division between husband and wife.

questionEn: In Surah Ar-Ra'd 13:11, what is the role of 'Al-Mu'aqqibat'—the successive angels before and behind each human being?
optionsEn: They erase sins automatically at midnight
They dictate poetry to scholars
They bring rain to private gardens
They guard the person by the command of Allah (yahfazunahu min amrillah)
explanationEn: Angels alternate in shifts guarding people by Allah's decree until an appointed fate arrives—immediately preceding the famous verse that Allah does not change a people's condition until they change themselves.

questionEn: According to Surah Ar-Rahman 55:15 and Sahih Muslim, from what distinct substances were the Jinn and Angels created respectively?
optionsEn: Jinn from black clay, and Angels from iron
Both Jinn and Angels from molten copper
Jinn from sea foam, and Angels from wind
Jinn from a smokeless flame of fire (marijin min nar), and Angels from light
explanationEn: The Qur'an specifies Jinn were created from smokeless fire (55:15; 15:27) and humans from clay, while the Prophet (peace be upon him) informed us that angels were created from light.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Mutaffifin 83:27-28 and Surah Al-Insan 76:18, what are 'Tasnim' and 'Salsabil'?
optionsEn: Two valleys in the Sinai desert
Exalted springs of Paradise from which the righteous drink
Two types of sacrificial camels
Two gates of the city of Madinah
explanationEn: Salsabil is a ginger-flavored spring in Paradise (76:17-18), while Tasnim is the noblest elevated fountain from which those brought nearest to Allah (Al-Muqarrabun) drink directly.

questionEn: In Surah An-Najm 53:14-16, what sacred landmark in the highest heavens is near the Garden of Refuge (Jannat al-Ma'wa)?
optionsEn: Al-Kawthar Bridge
Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary)
Al-Bayt al-Haram
Mount Tur of Sinai
explanationEn: During the Ascension (Mi'raj), the Prophet saw Jibril in his true form a second time at Sidrat al-Muntaha, beside which lies Jannat al-Ma'wa.

questionEn: In Surah Al-A'raf 7:43 and Surah Al-Hijr 15:47, what emotional purification does Allah perform in the chests of the inhabitants of Paradise?
optionsEn: He removes their ability to speak in groups
He erases all memory of their prayers on earth
He removes every trace of rancor or ill-feeling (ghill) so they sit as brothers facing one another on thrones
He makes them forget their parents' names
explanationEn: Any lingering resentment or worldly friction is completely cleansed from believers' hearts so that Paradise is filled with pure brotherhood and peace.

questionEn: Which lofty abode of Paradise is named 'Al-Firdaws' in Surah Al-Kahf 18:107 and Surah Al-Mu'minun 23:11?
optionsEn: An underground spring beneath Makkah
A temporary resting place outside the gates
A valley reserved solely for angels
The highest, finest gardens inherited by those who believe, do righteous deeds, guard prayer, and keep trusts
explanationEn: Surah Al-Mu'minun opens by listing the seven noble traits of successful believers, concluding: 'Those are the inheritors who will inherit Al-Firdaws; they will abide therein forever.'

questionEn: According to Surah At-Tawbah 9:72 and Surah Al-Qiyamah 75:22-23, what surpasses even the physical gardens and rivers as the supreme joy of Paradise?
optionsEn: Building seven palaces of pearl
Allah's Pleasure (Ridwan) and gazing upon the Countenance of their Lord
Riding winged horses across clouds
Owning mountains of emeralds
explanationEn: 'Wa ridwanun minAllahi akbar' (Allah's good pleasure is greater still), and radiant faces in Paradise will gaze joyfully upon their Lord.

questionEn: How does Surah As-Saffat 37:62-66 describe the Tree of Zaqqum in Hellfire?
optionsEn: A leafless oak growing in cold snow
A withered fig tree near the outer wall
A thornless lotus tree yielding bitter juice
A tree emerging from the bottom of Hellfire whose fruit-stalks look like the heads of devils
explanationEn: Placed as a trial for wrongdoers, Zaqqum grows in the depths of Hellfire; its food boils in bellies like molten brass (44:43-46).

questionEn: According to Surah Al-Hijr 15:44, how many gates does Jahannam (Hellfire) have?
optionsEn: Twelve gates corresponding to tribes
One single narrow gate
Three gates facing north
Seven gates, each with an assigned portion
explanationEn: Allah states: 'It has seven gates; for every gate is of them a portion designated,' reflecting graded levels of punishment matching levels of sin.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Mu'minun 23:99-100, what is 'Barzakh'?
optionsEn: A bridge spanning the Euphrates River
The barrier behind the dead preventing them from returning to this world until the Day of Resurrection
The name of the trumpet blown by Israfil
The golden scale used to weigh deeds
explanationEn: When death reaches a wrongdoer and they beg 'My Lord, send me back so I may do righteousness,' they are told 'No!'—for behind them is a Barzakh (barrier/intermediate realm) until Resurrection.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:177, what does Allah clarify that true righteousness (Al-Birr) is NOT confined to, before listing pillars of creed, charity, prayer, integrity, and patience?
optionsEn: Wearing coarse woolen garments
Speaking only in classical poetry
Merely turning your faces toward the east or the west
Giving gold coins to kings
explanationEn: Revealed around the Qiblah change, Ayat al-Birr teaches that outward direction means nothing without sincere faith, selfless charity, worship, keeping covenants, and perseverance.

questionEn: In Surah An-Nisa 4:135 and Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:8, what high standard of justice ('Adl) does the Qur'an demand from believers?
optionsEn: Avoiding testimony whenever disputes arise
Standing firm in justice even against oneself, parents, or kin, and never letting hatred of a people push one into injustice
Favoring one's own relatives in court
Judging harshly only against foreigners
explanationEn: Qur'anic justice transcends kinship and enmity alike: 'Be just; that is nearer to Taqwa' (5:8), even if testimony goes against one's own self or close family (4:135).

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hujurat 49:6, what ethical duty does Allah command believers when an untrustworthy person (fasiq) brings a piece of news?
optionsEn: Verify/investigate it carefully (fa-tabayyanu) lest you harm a people out of ignorance and regret it
Assume every rumor about outsiders is true
Share it immediately with everyone in the mosque
Punish the messenger before checking the facts
explanationEn: This foundational verse establishes rigorous media and social responsibility: never act upon or spread unverified claims that could unjustly injure innocent people.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hujurat 49:11, which three verbal and social harms are explicitly forbidden among believing men and women?
optionsEn: Bargaining, traveling, and lending
Mocking/ridiculing others, defaming one another, and calling offensive nicknames
Writing letters, greeting neighbors, and gifting dates
Debating grammar, reciting loudly, and fasting Mondays
explanationEn: Allah warns that those mocked might be better than the mockers, forbids hurting one's own community through slander, and condemns insulting nicknames—urging repentance.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Isra 17:23 and Surah Luqman 31:15, what is a believer commanded to do if non-Muslim parents pressure them to associate partners with Allah?
optionsEn: Sever all contact and refuse them food
Obey them temporarily to keep family peace
Refuse obedience in shirk, yet still accompany them in this world with kindness and fairness (ma'rufa)
Argue with them angrily every morning
explanationEn: While Tawhid takes absolute priority over parental obedience, Islam strictly preserves kindness, respect, and worldly care toward parents even across religious disagreement.

questionEn: In Surah Fussilat 41:34, what remarkable social transformation is promised when a believer 'repels evil with what is better' (idfa' billati hiya ahsan)?
optionsEn: One between whom and you was enmity becomes as though an intimate, devoted friend
Wealth doubles within seven nights
The adversary flees the country permanently
The dispute is forgotten in fifty years
explanationEn: Responding to hostility with dignity, patience, and goodness melts hardened animosity—a quality Allah notes is granted only to those who exercise patience and possess great good fortune.

questionEn: How strongly does Surah Al-Isra 17:26-27 condemn squandering wealth wastefully (tabdhir)?
optionsEn: It classifies squandering as a minor slip in etiquette
It says squandering increases a city's prestige
It calls the squanderers 'brothers of the devils' (ikhwanash-shayatin)
It permits squandering only during weddings
explanationEn: After commanding kindness to relatives, the needy, and the stranded traveler, Allah forbids wasteful spending—reminding believers that Satan is ever ungrateful to his Lord.

questionEn: Which two fundamental civic obligations are paired together in Surah An-Nisa 4:58?
optionsEn: Rendering trusts (amanat) back to their rightful owners and judging among people with justice
Planting date palms and digging wells
Collecting tolls and guarding bridges
Building forts and minting coins
explanationEn: Addressed to every individual and leader alike, 4:58 establishes trustworthiness and impartial justice as cornerstones of an ethical Islamic society.

questionEn: In Surah An-Nur 24:27-28, what must a visitor do if they ask permission to enter another person's home and are told 'Go back' (irji'u)?
optionsEn: Insist three more times until admitted
Enter through the courtyard instead
Wait silently behind the curtain until sunset
Turn back immediately, for that is purer for them
explanationEn: The Qur'an protects domestic privacy strictly: never enter another's house without permission and greeting, and depart gracefully without resentment if asked to leave.

questionEn: Which governance and community principle is praised in Surah Ash-Shura 42:38 alongside establishing prayer and spending from provision?
optionsEn: Secret unilateral decrees
Conducting their affairs through mutual consultation (wa amruhum shura baynahum)
Hereditary silence
Annual lottery selection
explanationEn: Shura (mutual consultation) is enshrined as a hallmark of the believing community—even the Prophet himself was instructed in 3:159 to consult his companions.

questionEn: In Surah Luqman 31:18-19, what everyday manners did Luqman the Wise teach his son regarding walking and speaking?
optionsEn: Walk swiftly with head raised high and speak louder than elders
Be moderate in your pace and lower your voice—for the harshest of voices is that of donkeys
Walk only on paved stone roads
Never speak in public markets
explanationEn: After warning against turning one's cheek in arrogance or walking boastfully on earth, Luqman taught balanced humility in movement and gentle restraint in speech.

questionEn: What manner of speech did Allah command Musa and Harun to use even when addressing the tyrant Pharaoh in Surah Ta-Ha 20:44?
optionsEn: Riddles hidden in poetry
Gentle speech (qawlan layyinan), so that perhaps he might be reminded or fear Allah
Harsh denunciations at the palace gate
Complete silence until a miracle occurred
explanationEn: If Allah commanded gentle, dignified speech toward one who claimed divinity ('I am your highest lord'), how much more does da'wah and everyday dialogue require gentleness!

questionEn: In Surah An-Nisa 4:140, what must believers do if they hear the verses of Allah being disbelieved in and mocked in a gathering?
optionsEn: Do not sit with them until they enter into another conversation
Join quietly to avoid awkwardness
Argue loudly until midnight
Cover their eyes without leaving
explanationEn: Remaining silently present while revelation is ridiculed makes one complicit in the gathering; believers are instructed to excuse themselves until the topic shifts.

questionEn: In Surah An-Nur 24:30-31, what sequence of personal modesty is commanded first to believing men and then to believing women?
optionsEn: Avoid speaking to neighbors altogether
Fast every alternate day
Travel only during winter months
Lower their gaze and guard their chastity (yaghuddu min absarihim wa yahfazu furujahum)
explanationEn: Islam addresses the root of moral purity in both men and women equally: restraining the gaze and safeguarding chastity, noting 'that is purer for them.'

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:124, when Allah made Prophet Ibrahim a leader (Imam) for mankind and Ibrahim asked 'And of my descendants?', how did Allah reply?
optionsEn: 'Only your eldest son will inherit leadership'
'All of your descendants will be prophets'
'Your descendants will rule only for five centuries'
'My covenant does not include the wrongdoers (az-zalimin)'
explanationEn: Allah established a timeless moral principle: spiritual leadership and divine covenant are earned through righteousness, never merely blood lineage.

questionEn: What three categories of worshippers did Allah command Ibrahim and Isma'il to purify His House for in Surah Al-Baqarah 2:125?
optionsEn: Fasters, travelers, and farmers
Scholars, judges, and scribes
Merchants, poets, and guards
Those who perform Tawaf (at-ta'ifin), those staying in devotion (al-'akifin), and those who bow and prostrate (ar-rukka'is-sujud)
explanationEn: Both physical cleanliness and spiritual purity from idolatry were mandated for the Sacred House to serve visitors circling it, residing in worship, and praying.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:126, how did Allah respond when Prophet Ibrahim prayed for Makkah's believing residents to be provided with fruits—and asked about disbelievers?
optionsEn: Allah promised only believers would ever taste rain or fruit in Arabia
Allah affirmed He gives worldly enjoyment briefly even to disbelievers, before compelling them to the Fire
Allah restricted fruits exclusively to Madinah
Allah stated no trade caravans would visit Makkah
explanationEn: Out of universal mercy in worldly sustenance, Allah provides for both believers and disbelievers in this life, while ultimate reward and accountability belong to the Hereafter.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:142, what foundational truth did Allah instruct the Prophet to reply when critics questioned the change of Qiblah from Jerusalem to Makkah?
optionsEn: 'The stars changed their alignment in winter'
'To Allah belong the east and the west; He guides whom He wills to a straight path'
'Jerusalem was only for night prayers'
'Makkah is closer to the Red Sea'
explanationEn: Every direction belongs to Allah; facing a Qiblah is an act of loving obedience to Allah's command rather than believing Allah is physically confined to one direction.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:143, directly connected to the Qiblah change, what title did Allah bestow upon the Muslim community—and why had He originally appointed the first Qiblah?
optionsEn: A silent community; to hide their prayers from Byzantium
A nomadic community; to simplify navigation
A justly balanced community (Ummatan Wasatan); to test who follows the Messenger versus who turns back on his heels
A lunar community; to count the sacred months
explanationEn: The shift of Qiblah served as a decisive test of loyalty to the Messenger over tribal or habitual attachment, establishing the Muslims as a balanced witness community.

questionEn: What longing of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is captured in Surah Al-Baqarah 2:144 right before the command to face Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: Fasting continuously for three months
Digging wells around Quba
Writing letters to Abyssinia
Repeatedly turning his face toward the sky awaiting revelation (taqalluba wajhika fis-sama')
explanationEn: Out of modesty and devotion, the Prophet did not explicitly demand the change, instead gazing hopefully skyward—and Allah honored him by turning him to the Qiblah of Ibrahim.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:148, immediately following the verses on Qiblah, what constructive counsel does Allah give believers?
optionsEn: 'Build walls facing only the southern sky'
'Stop traveling outside Madinah for two years'
'Debate the people of Jerusalem every afternoon'
'Every community has a direction toward which it turns, so race to all that is good (fastabiqul-khayrat)'
explanationEn: Rather than getting bogged down in endless polemics over direction, believers are urged to channel their energy into excelling in good deeds.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:189, what two purposes do the crescent moons (al-ahillah) serve, and what pre-Islamic Hajj superstition did the same verse correct?
optionsEn: Predicting rain and planting wheat; forbidding night travel
Counting years of kings; forbidding walking barefoot
Timing eclipses and tides; forbidding wearing white wool
Measuring time for people and Hajj (mawaqit); clarifying that piety is not entering houses from their backs during Ihram
explanationEn: Some tribes used to climb through rear holes of their homes while in Ihram thinking it pious; Allah corrected this, teaching that true righteousness is Taqwa.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:191, under what sole condition is fighting permitted near Al-Masjid al-Haram, and why?
optionsEn: Whenever merchants raise prices
During any winter caravan season
Only if aggressors fight you there first—and oppression/persecution (fitnah) is worse than killing
Only after sunset on Fridays
explanationEn: Al-Masjid al-Haram is an inviolable sanctuary where fighting is forbidden unless forced in self-defense against those who violate its sanctity first.

questionEn: What foundational rule of pilgrimage commitment is established by the opening words of Surah Al-Baqarah 2:196: 'Wa atimmul-Hajja wal-'Umrata lillah'?
optionsEn: Hajj and Umrah must always be separated by six months
Umrah may only be performed once every ten years
Pilgrims must fast every day of their journey
Once a person enters Ihram for Hajj or Umrah, they are obligated to complete its rites for Allah (unless prevented)
explanationEn: Scholars derive from this command that unlike voluntary prayers or fasts, entering Ihram for even a voluntary Hajj or Umrah obligates completing it fully for Allah.

questionEn: According to Surah Al-Baqarah 2:196, if a pilgrim in Ihram is blocked from reaching the Sacred House (ihsar), what must they do before shaving their head and exiting Ihram?
optionsEn: Send whatever sacrificial animal (hady) is easy to obtain, and not shave the head until the hady reaches its place of sacrifice
Pay a silver coin to the tribe at the border
Walk backwards to Madinah
Wait inside a tent for forty days
explanationEn: This verse guided the Prophet and his companions at Hudaybiyyah when prevented from entering Makkah—sending/sacrificing their hady before shaving and exiting Ihram.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:196, if an ill pilgrim must shave their head early during Ihram, what three options of Fidyah (expiation) are mentioned in the verse?
optionsEn: Returning home immediately, paying double tax, or remaining silent
Reciting three surahs, donating a cloak, or releasing a bird
Fasting, charity, or a sacrifice (min siyamin aw sadaqatin aw nusuk)
Walking around the Ka'bah twice, giving water, or planting a palm
explanationEn: Revealed regarding Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah (RA), the Prophet explained these three options as fasting 3 days, feeding 6 needy people, or sacrificing a sheep.

questionEn: Who is exempt from the Tamattu' sacrificial animal (hady) obligation mentioned in Surah Al-Baqarah 2:196?
optionsEn: Scholars teaching in Mina
Pilgrims over the age of sixty
Pilgrims traveling by sea
Those whose family/residence is among those present at Al-Masjid al-Haram (locals of Makkah)
explanationEn: The verse concludes: 'That is for whoever's family is not in the area of Al-Masjid al-Haram,' exempting Makkah residents from the Tamattu' sacrifice.

questionEn: Which three specific behaviors are prohibited for anyone who undertakes Hajj in Surah Al-Baqarah 2:197?
optionsEn: Trading, sleeping after noon, and speaking Arabic
Eating honey, wearing sandals, and drinking cold water
Sexual indecency/relations (rafath), sinful disobedience (fusuq), and quarrelling/disputing (jidal)
Writing letters, carrying luggage, and riding camels
explanationEn: Pilgrimage trains total self-restraint: abstaining from marital intimacy, all forms of sin, and heated arguments preserves the sanctity and reward of Hajj.

questionEn: What spiritual lesson lies behind the command 'Take provisions, and indeed the best provision is Taqwa' in Surah Al-Baqarah 2:197?
optionsEn: While taking practical travel provisions so one does not burden others, God-consciousness (Taqwa) is the truest provision for the journey to Allah
Pilgrims should fast throughout the entire journey to save food
Pilgrims must carry gold coins instead of silver
Only wealthy merchants should travel to Makkah
explanationEn: Revealed when some travelers from Yemen set out without supplies claiming reliance on Allah and ended up begging, this ayah balances worldly preparation with inner Taqwa.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:198, what misconception did Allah remove by stating 'There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord' during Hajj?
optionsEn: That engaging in lawful trade and commerce during the Hajj season is sinful
That praying outside the mosque in Arafat is invalid
That drinking Zamzam water breaks fasting
That riding animals to Mina is disliked
explanationEn: Early Muslims worried that buying and selling at Hajj markets like 'Ukaz and Dhul-Majaz might taint their worship; Allah confirmed lawful trade during Hajj is permissible.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:198-199, where are pilgrims instructed to remember Allah upon departing from 'Arafat, and what pre-Islamic arrogance did verse 199 abolish?
optionsEn: At Al-Mash'ar al-Haram (Muzdalifah); abolishing Quraysh's elitist habit of stopping at Muzdalifah instead of standing at 'Arafat with everyone else
At Mount Uhud; abolishing tribal banners
At Wadi Fatima; abolishing night travel
At Quba; abolishing riding horses
explanationEn: Quraysh used to claim superiority as 'Al-Hums' and refused to stand outside the Haram boundary at 'Arafat; Allah commanded all pilgrims equally to stand at 'Arafat and depart together.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:200-202, how does the Qur'an contrast two kinds of pilgrims making du'a after completing their rites?
optionsEn: One prays silently and one prays aloud
One prays standing on Safa and the other on Marwah
One asks only for worldly benefits (leaving no share in the Hereafter), while the other prays for good in this world, good in the Hereafter, and protection from the Fire
One prays in Arabic and one in Aramaic
explanationEn: Pre-Islamic pilgrims used to boast of ancestors and ask only for rain, livestock, or victory; Islam redirected pilgrim supplication to embrace both worlds and salvation.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:203, during the 'appointed days' (Ayyam Ma'dudat—the Days of Tashriq in Mina), what flexibility is granted regarding when a pilgrim may depart?
optionsEn: Everyone is required to stay for seven full days
Everyone must leave before sunrise on the 10th
Whoever hastens away in two days (12th Dhul-Hijjah) incurs no sin, and whoever delays (13th) incurs no sin, for whoever fears Allah
Only Makkah residents may leave early
explanationEn: Remembering Allah during the Days of Tashriq (at Jamarat and throughout Mina) includes compassionate flexibility for either early departure on the 12th or staying through the 13th.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Baqarah 2:217, when asked about fighting in the Sacred Month, what did Allah declare is 'even graver with Allah' than fighting?
optionsEn: Preventing people from Allah's path, disbelief in Him, barring access to Al-Masjid al-Haram, and expelling its inhabitants
Speaking loudly near the Ka'bah
Delaying a caravan by one day
Missing a trade fair in Yemen
explanationEn: While respecting the Sacred Months is serious, Quraysh's systematic persecution, expelling believers from their homes, and blocking them from the Sacred Mosque was far graver before Allah.

questionEn: In Surah Al-'Imran 3:96, what ancient name is used for Makkah when declaring the Ka'bah the first house of worship established for mankind?
optionsEn: Bakkah
Yathrib
Iram
Madyan
explanationEn: Surah Al-'Imran 3:96 states: 'Indeed, the first House [of worship] established for mankind was that at Bakkah—blessed and a guidance for the worlds.'

questionEn: In Surah Al-'Imran 3:97, what phrase defines the condition upon which Hajj to the House is obligatory upon mankind?
optionsEn: Whoever has memorized half the Qur'an
Whoever owns a camel and a tent
Whoever lives within ten days' ride
Whoever is able to find a way thereto (manistata'a ilayhi sabila)
explanationEn: Islamic scholars explain 'istita'ah' (ability) covers physical health, financial means for the journey and dependents left behind, and safe passage.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:2, what sacred symbols and offerings related to pilgrimage are believers strictly warned NOT to violate?
optionsEn: The symbols of Allah (sha'a'irillah), the sacred month, the sacrificial animals (hady), the garlanded offerings (qala'id), and people heading to the Sacred House
The ships sailing in the Mediterranean
The cedar trees of Lebanon
The city walls of Damascus
explanationEn: Even during tense hostilities, believers were strictly commanded not to let hatred cause them to violate sacred pilgrimage rites or pilgrims peacefully heading to the House.

questionEn: According to Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:95, if a pilgrim in Ihram intentionally kills land game, what is the primary penalty prescribed?
optionsEn: Repeating the entire Hajj the following year
Shaving one's beard and paying ten gold dinars
Immediate expulsion from Makkah for five years
An equivalent domestic animal judged by two just persons among you as a sacrificial offering to reach the Ka'bah, or feeding the poor / equivalent fasting
explanationEn: Sanctity of life in Ihram and the Haram extends to wild land animals; violating it requires an equivalent livestock offering for the poor of the Haram or proportional feeding/fasting.

questionEn: Which category of game is explicitly declared lawful for pilgrims to catch and eat even while in Ihram according to Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:96?
optionsEn: Wild doves inside Makkah
Desert ostriches
Mountain ibex
Game of the sea and its food (saydul-bahri wa ta'amuh)
explanationEn: While land game (saydul-barr) is forbidden throughout Ihram, fish and sea food remain completely lawful as sustenance for travelers and residents alike.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:97, what does Allah declare He has made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, to be for humanity?
optionsEn: A museum of ancient inscriptions
A private sanctuary for one tribe
A seasonal fortress for caravans
An enduring support and standard for mankind (qiyaman lin-nas)
explanationEn: Along with the Sacred Month, the Hady, and garlanded offerings, the Ka'bah serves as a spiritual and social anchor upholding humanity's worship, peace, and livelihood.

questionEn: In Surah At-Tawbah 9:28, when polytheists were barred from approaching Al-Masjid al-Haram after 9 AH, how did Allah reassure Muslims who feared economic loss from reduced pilgrimage trade?
optionsEn: He promised: 'If you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty if He wills'
He permitted charging pilgrims entry tolls
He ordered them to mine silver in Ta'if
He told them to abandon Makkah for Yemen
explanationEn: Purifying the Sacred Sanctuary of idolatry never harmed Makkah's livelihood; instead, Muslims from across the globe brought unprecedented spiritual and material blessings.

questionEn: In Surah At-Tawbah 9:36, how many months are Sacred Months (Al-Ashhur al-Hurum) out of the twelve months ordained by Allah since creation?
optionsEn: Three sacred months (Shawwal, Dhul-Qa'dah, and Dhul-Hijjah)
Six sacred months alternating all year
Four sacred months (Dhul-Qa'dah, Dhul-Hijjah, Muharram, and Rajab)
Two sacred months (Ramadan and Dhul-Hijjah)
explanationEn: The Qur'an specifies four out of twelve months as sacred, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) identified them during the Farewell Pilgrimage as three consecutive (Dhul-Qa'dah, Dhul-Hijjah, Muharram) and one solitary (Rajab).

questionEn: What pre-Islamic manipulation of the sacred calendar is condemned in Surah At-Tawbah 9:37 as 'an increase in disbelief'?
optionsEn: Starting the year in spring
An-Nasi'—postponing or swapping a sacred month to another month to make fighting lawful
Fasting on the tenth of Muharram
Counting months by solar equinoxes
explanationEn: When tribes wanted to raid during Muharram, they declared it ordinary and pushed its sanctity to Safar; Allah abolished this tampering completely.

questionEn: In Surah At-Tawbah 9:19, how does the Qur'an evaluate providing water to pilgrims (siqayatal-hajj) and maintaining Al-Masjid al-Haram compared to sincere faith and striving in Allah's cause?
optionsEn: Maintaining the mosque is forbidden for anyone who travels
Both carry the exact same reward without faith
Providing water to pilgrims automatically outranks everything
They are NOT equal—those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, and strive in Allah's path are far greater in degree with Allah
explanationEn: When Makkan polytheists boasted of serving water to pilgrims and tending the Ka'bah, Allah clarified that outward service devoid of Tawhid and sacrifice cannot equal sincere faith.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hajj 22:25, what two groups are declared to have equal rights in Al-Masjid al-Haram?
optionsEn: Traders and sailors
Scholars and poets
Kings and governors only
The local resident (al-'akif) and the visitor from afar (al-bad)
explanationEn: Allah explicitly forbids monopolizing the Sacred Mosque and warns that anyone who merely intends deviation with wrongdoing there will taste a painful punishment.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hajj 22:27, how did Allah describe the response to Prophet Ibrahim's proclamation of the Hajj to mankind?
optionsEn: They will send letters instead of traveling in person
They will come only from the hills surrounding Makkah
They will come on foot (rijalan) and on every lean camel (kulli damir), coming from every distant mountain pass (min kulli fajjin 'amiq)
They will arrive exclusively during full eclipses
explanationEn: Centuries before modern transit, Allah foretold that pilgrims would travel across vast distances and lean mounts from every remote corner of the earth.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hajj 22:28, what two purposes are stated for pilgrims arriving at the Sacred House?
optionsEn: To collect stones from Mount Safa
To debate genealogy and compose odes
To witness benefits for themselves (spiritual and worldly) and mention Allah's name on known days over sacrificial livestock, eating and feeding the distressed poor
To crown tribal kings and trade silk
explanationEn: Hajj unites worship, gratitude, brotherhood, lawful benefit, and tangible generosity toward the poor and needy.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hajj 22:29, what three concluding actions are commanded of pilgrims as they complete their Hajj rites?
optionsEn: End their untidiness (li-yaqdu tafathahum—shaving/trimming), fulfill their vows, and circumambulate the Ancient House (Al-Bayt al-'Atiq)
Wash their cloaks in Zamzam, donate silver, and rest three days
Build a tent in Mina, light lamps, and write their names
Fast seven days, climb Mount Hira, and leave Makkah quietly
explanationEn: Following the sacrifice on the Day of Nahr, pilgrims exit Ihram restrictions (shaving/clipping hair and nails), fulfill vows, and perform Tawaf al-Ifadah around the Ancient House.

questionEn: According to Surah Al-Hajj 22:32, what inward quality of the heart is demonstrated when a believer honors the symbols of Allah (sha'a'irAllah)?
optionsEn: Physical endurance
The piety of the hearts (taqwal-qulub)
Tribal pride
Commercial shrewdness
explanationEn: Respecting sacred times, places, rites, and sacrificial offerings springs directly from reverence and God-consciousness inside the heart.

questionEn: In Surah Al-Hajj 22:36, which two categories of needy people are pilgrims commanded to feed from the meat of sacrificial camels (al-budn)?
optionsEn: The contented poor who refrains from begging (al-qani') and the needy person who asks/presents himself (al-mu'tarr)
Only one's own wealthy relatives
Caravan leaders and camel drivers
Only soldiers and guards
explanationEn: Islam teaches sensitivity to both the dignified poor who suffer silently without asking and those who openly request help.

questionEn: What spiritual reality about pilgrimage sacrifice is immortalized in Surah Al-Hajj 22:37?
optionsEn: Only the largest camels are accepted by Allah
The blood must be sprinkled on the Ka'bah walls
Neither their meat nor their blood reaches Allah, but it is your Taqwa (piety) that reaches Him
Meat must never be eaten by the pilgrim who offered it
